title: Protocol for Determining Gut Microbiota Metabolites in Mouse Metabolism
author: Fang, Kukje Zada, et al.

steps.title: Power on and launch analyzer
steps.instruction: Switch on the power button on the side of the stable‑isotope gas analyzer; the launch service screen will appear. Click the launch button (CCIA) to start the analyzer (the analyzer will auto‑launch after 120 s of inactivity).

steps.title: Activate vacuum pump and set pressure
steps.instruction: Turn on the vacuum pump and adjust the vacuum pressure to approximately 120 Torr (the pressure is displayed in Promethion Live when the analyzer is connected to the CGF).

steps.title: Select display and recording settings
steps.instruction: Click the Display tab (bottom left) and choose one of the four display screens (numeric, alarm status, spectrum, time chart). Click the Rate tab (bottom left) and set the data‑recording frequency to the default 1 s (recommended to match Promethion measurements). Open the Setup tab (bottom right), select the Time/Files tab, and set the baud rate to 115200 and the correct time zone. Do NOT change any Calibration settings without expert supervision. The Laser Adjust, MIU, DCS, and Service screens are not used.

steps.title: Close setup and access data files
steps.instruction: Click the Close button to return to the home screens, then click the Files tab (bottom right) to access the recorded data (normally logged automatically by the Promethion system).

steps.title: Shut down analyzer and pump
steps.instruction: Click the Exit button followed by the Shutdown button to turn off the analyzer. Afterwards, turn off the vacuum pump and switch off the analyzer completely.

steps.title: Download and export raw data
steps.instruction: After the recording is finished, download the data from Promethion Live. Use MacroInterpreter with the standard analytical scripts to process the raw data and export it as an Excel file (e.g., a file from a mouse given 2.5 mg of 1‑13C glucose).

steps.title: Calculate tracer oxidation rate
steps.instruction: Perform the following calculations using the exported Excel file:

substeps.instruction: Identify the two required columns: VCO₂ (vco2) and 13C enrichment in exhaled CO₂ (si13c).
Set the time of tracer administration to 0 min for each mouse.
Compute the average VCO₂ and si13c values for the one‑hour period preceding tracer administration; this is the baseline (0 min).
Determine the time point when si13c returns to the baseline value; this indicates complete tracer oxidation.
Convert si13c to Atom Percent (AP) using: AP = 100 × ((si13c/1000) + 1) × 0.0112372 + 1 (0.0112372 is the Pee Dee Belemnite standard for ¹³C/¹²C).
Calculate Atom Fraction Excess (AFE): AFE = (AP_sample – AP_baseline) / 100.
Compute the tracer oxidation rate (T) with: T = VCO₂ × AFE × q × k × m, where:
q = number of ¹³C atoms in the tracer,
k = volume of CO₂ produced per mg of tracer oxidized (mL · mg⁻¹); use literature values (e.g., from McCue et al.) or set k = 1 if the animal burns a mixture of fuels,
m = molecular weight of the tracer.
Calculate cumulative tracer oxidation as the area under the curve of the oxidation‑rate trace.
Perform statistical analysis on the cumulative oxidation values (e.g., t‑tests or one‑way ANOVA depending on the number of experimental groups).

description: Gut microbiota produces various metabolites that can serve as substrates for host metabolic pathways.2 As an example, both bacteria and host tissues can produce either enantiomer of lactate. L-lactate is mainly produced in the host, primarily in the muscle, which fuels the Cori cycle. We found that bacteria produce most of the D-lactate that is circulating in mice. We determined whether D-lactate originating from gut bacteria can also serve as a fuel source for host glucose metabolism via an alternate branch in the Cori cycle. Although methods existed to track the fate of stable isotope-labeled exogenous substrates, we devised a method to track endogenously produced metabolites derived from the gut microbiota, which then can be used by the host. In this protocol, we measured a stable isotope of carbon in exhaled breath of mice after “feeding” bacteria in the gut using oral gavage in order to reveal the oxidation of labeled substrates.3 We first measured 13C-labeled lactulose in bacterial culture, where it is metabolized by commensals to produce 13C-labeled D-lactate. Next, we orally administered 13C-labeled lactulose, which cannot be processed by the host, to specific pathogen-free (SPF) mice, monocolonized mice, and germ-free (GF) mice to monitor 13CO2 production in free moving mice. This two-step strategy provides evidence that microbial-derived D-lactate can be utilized by the host as a fuel source for glucose metabolism. Although this protocol is exemplified using microbial-derived D-lactate, it can be readily adapted to other microbial-derived metabolites, provided that selected substates are exclusively metabolized by microbial enzymes and not by host pathways. Furthermore, this protocol is compatible with the use of 18O-labeled substrates.
